text: On March 3, 2026, the City Council approved a construction contract to begin building a new community center and event hall at Fremont’s Central Park. Originally envisioned as being built in two phases as separate projects—with a new community center as phase 1 and an adjoining event hall as phase 2—the City is taking advantage of a favorable bidding climate for new building construction and is saving money by constructing a larger project all at once. The $51 million project is located just south of the Fremont Main Library and will replace the existing Teen Center. Features of the project include: ■New Community Center with flexible indoor spaces for fitness, dance, arts, crafts, enrichment, STEM learning, and a community meeting room. In This Issue Budget Charter City ■New Outdoor Living Room with patios, furnishings, and shade features to provide social and relaxation spaces, and accommodations for a mobile coffee/snack cart and food trucks. ■New Event Hall, Outdoor Event Patio, and Terrace with a commercial kitchen, indoor seating capacity for 400 people; an adjoining outdoor patio with table seating capacity for an additional 200 people (600 total); and a ceremonial lawn for weddings and other events, featuring views of Lake Elizabeth and Mission Peak. The project is planned to start construction in Spring 2026 and be opened in Spring 2028. A ground-breaking ceremony is scheduled for April 17, 2026. text: Fremont City Council Charter Advisory Committee On February 17, 2026, the Fremont City Council initiated the process for proposing a new City Charter to be completed in time to be placed on the ballot for consideration by Fremont voters in November 2026. To achieve this outcome, the Mayor appointed, and the City Council ratified, a 7-member Charter Advisory Committee in March to help provide structured input. In compliance with the Brown Act, the Committee will meet during noticed public meetings to complete its work and provide recommendations to the City Council. The Committee will review the Charter formation process, the City’s existing government structure and operations and research best practices on key issues and potential topics that may be addressed by a Charter. The City Council has identified several priorities including: ■Governance models ■Hiring authority ■Meeting structures ■Principles of accountability, transparency, and non-interference ■Term limits options ■Council compensation considerations ■City Council staffing options After the Committee finalizes its recommendations, a proposed Charter document will be drafted and presented to City Council for consideration at a minimum of two public hearings and a third meeting for a final vote of the Council prior to it being placed on the ballot by August 7, 2026. Stay Informed: fremont.gov/chartercity The City Continues to Adapt to a Dynamic Fiscal Landscape On June 10, 2025, the City Council adopted the Fiscal Year 2025/26 Operating Budget, ensuring it remained balanced by aligning expenditures with projected ongoing resources. The City successfully avoided tapping into the Budget Uncertainty Reserve, though infrastructure maintenance was trimmed by roughly $3 million. As labor negotiations were under way when the FY 2025/26 Operating Budget was prepared, the adopted budget did not include compensation increases. In January, the City finalized labor negotiations and reached one-year agreements with all nine bargaining units, which included a 1.3% cost of living adjustment and an additional monthly health benefit allowance. At the February 10, 2026, Council meeting, the Fremont City Council approved a rebalancing plan for the FY 2025/26 budget to address the additional ongoing personnel expenses. This adjustment included a $3.8 million increase in appropriations for personnel costs, offset by reductions in staffing, overtime, training, and contract services. While nine non-sworn police positions were permanently eliminated, the recommended personnel reductions did not result in layoffs. In early March, the City’s Finance Director presented City Council with the annual Mid-year Operating Budget report. The City’s preliminary revenue outlook assumes the economy will continue to grow, but persistently high mortgage rates are expected to dampen property sales and, consequently, property tax revenues, at least through the end of 2026. As preparations for next year’s budget begin, the focus remains on making prudent decisions that support the City Council’s Adopted Priorities while minimizing impact on staff. The City Council will be presented with the FY 2026/27 Proposed Operating Budget on May 12, 2026, followed by a budget hearing and adoption in early June. All Council meetings are televised on the local cable access channel (Ch 27), streamed online at city.fremont.gov/webcasts, or available to attend in person at City Hall, located at 3300 Capitol Ave. Meetings begin at 7 p.m.

Homeless Encampment Management The City continues to receive a high volume of requests for immediate intervention at vehicle and tent encampments throughout Fremont, and we would like to share information with the community on how homelessness concerns are addressed. The primary approach, outlined in the City Council-adopted Homelessness Response Plan, is to first approach concerns with housing and servicesbased strategies, including providing alternative shelter, to those at risk of displacement. This strategy was effective in our resolutions at Vallejo Mill in 2024 and, more recently at Isherwood Park, these combined efforts successfully transitioned more than 60 unhoused residents into shelter programs. However, given recent citywide budget rebalancing measures, the City does not currently have sufficient funding to implement housing and service-based strategies to provide adequate shelter for all individuals living in the remaining encampments. City staff most commonly conduct health and safety clean ups to mitigate waste accumulation or dangerous conditions. While enforcing the camping ordinance without corresponding service offerings is an option, the City would take such action only if conditions require emergency intervention, based on existing policy. Encampment closures without service offerings create cycles of hardship and don’t reduce homelessness. Individuals may lose connections with established service supports, their personal belongings, identification, and medications. Closures also make it more challenging to access jobs, healthcare,

To help address homelessness, in March the City Council adopted a new formal shelter crisis declaration. By taking this step, the City can accelerate the approval and construction of emergency housing facilities—commonly known as shelters— as the declaration provides exemptions from certain state laws. The declaration also strengthens Fremont’s position when applying for competitive funding designed to reduce homelessness. In addition, the City is prioritizing transparency. We're working on a new homelessness response dashboard to provide real-time data to help our community visualize and stay informed on how we are tracking toward Citywide goals. Rather than solving an individual’s homelessness status, closures without relocation options may shift the presence of encampments to more visible areas such as residential neighborhoods, or deeper into environmentally sensitive or hazardous locations. This repeated cycle strains City budgets and diverts limited public safety resources from lasting solutions, is chronically stressful for unhoused residents, and decreases effectiveness of outreach services. Our current hope is that the Alameda County Home Together Fund, funded through voter-approved Measure W, including the Cardea Health/ Abode project, will increase shelter beds in Southern Alameda County to accommodate the most vulnerable unhoused residents, and expand the capacity of the local shelter system to address entrenched encampments. Fremont Unified School District Updates

The City of Fremont Human Services Department and FUSD continue their long-standing partnership in providing programs, resources, and services to Fremont’s children and families. Currently, the City operates after school programs at six elementary schools promoting learning, social connections, and personal growth beyond the school day. Recognizing the importance of student mental health, FUSD also partners with the City to offer support services at five secondary schools, helping students build coping skills, strengthen resilience, and access support when needed. Families new to Fremont Unified are invited to apply for immediate enrollment or for the 2026–2027 school year. Learn more at fremontunified.org/enroll. text: A Clean Bay Begins Here Right here in Fremont, the storm drains you see on our streets connect directly to local creeks, ponds, lakes, wetlands, and the Bay, without going to a treatment plant first. This means that whatever goes down the storm drain (or “gutter”) can end up in our waterways. When rainfall flows into our storm drains, it carries pollution from our streets and sidewalks with it—such as litter, car wash water, and pet waste—spoiling Fremont’s natural beauty. The wildlife living in our waterways also depends on clean water to thrive. Since our storm drains lead directly to their habitats, keeping our streets and sidewalks clean is essential for their survival. Local species—including the steelhead and Chinook Some Fish Don’t Go With the Flow salmon spotted in Alameda Creek in recent years, as well as egrets, ducks, red-legged frogs, and freshwater turtles—rely on us. This is why the City of Fremont is partnering with the Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program and artist Joanna Sokua to encourage everyone to reduce pollution on our streets to protect our water. Learn more and pledge to take action at cleanwaterprogram.org/clean-bay. Did you know birds aren’t the only animals that migrate? Each year, several iconic fish species migrate through California’s extensive waterways. Anadromous fish hatch in freshwater and move downstream to the ocean, where abundant resources allow them to grow and mature. After months or sometimes years in saltwater, they begin a remarkable journey back to their original freshwater streams to lay their eggs in gravel beds and create the next generation. The ability for these fish to survive in such a wide range of salinity is noteworthy as most fish can only survive in one type of water. For some species, this migration cycle can be repeated multiple times, while for others it marks the end of their journey. In these cases, their sacrifice plays a vital ecological role by transporting marine-derived nutrients inland, enriching waterways and providing food for surrounding ecosystems. Locally, both steelhead and Chinook salmon are known to migrate through portions of Alameda Creek during their life cycle. For instance, in the fall of 2025, Chinook salmon traveled through Fremont to the Sunol Valley for the first time in decades. Despite their resilience, anadromous fish face significant barriers, such as dams, culverts, and habitat loss, which block migration routes and disrupt natural flows. As a result, restoration efforts and improving habitat connectivity are critical to supporting population recovery. To find out more about local anadromous fish and how you can help them, visit the City’s Nature Learning Center located at 40224 Paseo Padre Parkway in Fremont. For operating hours and more information, visit city.fremont.gov/nlc. Mercury, PCBs, and Your Plate: What Bay Area Fish Consumers Should Know Mercury and Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) are longlasting pollutants that linger in our environment. Mercury occurs naturally, but human activities such as chemical spills, industrial processes, and wastewater discharges have significantly increased its presence. PCBs, though production is banned, remain in electrical equipment, older buildings and infrastructure due to their previous widespread use in materials such as paint, insulation, and plastics. When these materials are damaged, improperly handled, or disposed of, stormwater can carry these contaminants into the San Francisco Bay. To help restore the Bay’s health, Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) standards have been established to limit mercury and PCB levels. TMDLs refer to how much of a pollutant can enter a U.S. waterbody while still maintaining its water quality standards. Elevated levels of mercury and PCB harm aquatic life, reduce biodiversity, and impair overall water quality. Keeping these pollutants out of the Bay is not just about protecting water quality, it also helps protect the fish we eat. Mercury and PCB can build up in fish over time, a process called bioaccumulation, which can pose risks to people who eat contaminated fish. Reducing pollutants at the source keeps fish healthier and lowers these risks. We can all play a part in this effort by disposing of waste properly and cleaning up any spills and leaks immediately. Fish can still be part of a healthy diet—offering protein, omega3s, and important vitamins—but they should be eaten in moderation, according to safety advisories. Fish consumption guidelines vary by waterbody, county, fish species, and demographic factors. Review California’s local advisories at oehha.ca.gov/fish. How to Dispose of Needles and Unwanted Medications in Fremont Items like needles, syringes, and expired medications require special handling and should never be placed in your trash, recycling, or compost carts. Proper disposal is essential to keeping our community safe, protecting healthcare and sanitation workers, and protecting the environment. Do NOT toss medications in the trash or toilet. Where do I take sharps (needles, syringes, and lancets)? In Fremont, sharps are accepted at: ■Local pharmacies (Haller's Pharmacy & Medical Supply) ■Hospitals (Kaiser and Washington Heath facilities) ■Household Hazardous Waste Facility at the Fremont Recycling and Transfer Station ■Mail-back option through sharpstakebackcalifornia.org Sharps must be in a puncture-resistant container with a secure lid before drop-off. Where do I take medications? In Fremont, expired/unwanted medications/pharmaceuticals are accepted at: ■Local pharmacies (Haller’s Pharmacy & Medical Supply and CVS) ■Hospitals (Kaiser and Washington Heath facilities) ■Special collection events, including the City’s upcoming Earth Day Fair and the annual Elks Lodge drug take back collection event Pour all unwanted pills into a sealable plastic bag. Keep ointments and liquids in their original containers. Bring medications to a medicine take-back site; call the site before bringing items for disposal. Reminder: The Household Hazardous Waste Facility at the Fremont Recycling and Transfer Station does NOT accept medical waste. I’m not sure where something goes. Where can I get more information? Visit resource.stopwaste.org to search by ZIP code and find even more local drop-off options for needles and medications, as well as hard-to-dispose items.
